title: Ankle arthritis: fusion or ankle replacement — which is right for me?
seoTitle: Ankle Arthritis: Fusion or Ankle Replacement?
metaDescription: Ankle arthritis explained: non-surgical care first, then ankle fusion vs total ankle replacement — walking, recovery, risks and what the TARVA trial found.
intro: Ankle arthritis is less common than knee or hip arthritis, and it often starts years after an old fracture or repeated sprains. Many people manage well without surgery. When pain from worn-out arthritis keeps limiting walking, the two main operations are ankle fusion and total ankle replacement. This guide explains how they compare, using the best evidence available.
summary: Start with non-surgical care: activity changes, weight loss, supportive or stiff-soled shoes, braces and sometimes an injection. If severe arthritis still limits daily life, both fusion and ankle replacement usually reduce pain. A UK randomised trial (TARVA) found similar one-year improvement, but each operation has different risks, so the choice depends on your ankle and lifestyle.

sections.heading: Why does ankle arthritis develop?
sections.body: Most ankle arthritis is post-traumatic: it follows an injury such as a fracture or dislocation that damaged the joint surface. AAOS OrthoInfo notes that an injured joint is about seven times more likely to become arthritic than an uninjured one. Wear-and-tear osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are other causes. The arthritis can appear many years after the original injury, so an ankle fracture or repeated sprains from your twenties may only cause trouble much later. If you are not sure whether an old injury was a sprain or a fracture, see our guide on ankle sprain vs fracture.

sections.heading: Can ankle arthritis be treated without surgery?
sections.body:
Yes, and this is where treatment should begin. AAOS OrthoInfo lists lifestyle changes, lower-impact exercise, weight loss, physiotherapy, braces, orthotics, stiff-soled or rocker-bottom shoes and anti-inflammatory medicines. A cortisone injection can help, but its effect is often temporary. Many people never need an operation.

Useful steps include:
bullets: Wearing well-cushioned shoes with a firm sole; an ankle brace or custom shoe can reduce painful movement
Losing weight if you are overweight, which reduces load on the ankle
Physiotherapy for strength and balance, stopping if it clearly worsens joint pain
Talking to your surgeon about which day-to-day positions, such as sitting cross-legged on the floor or squatting, are sensible for your ankle

sections.heading: Is keyhole (arthroscopic) surgery useful?
sections.body: Keyhole surgery can help in early arthritis, when pain comes mainly from bone spurs at the front of the ankle and the joint space is still fairly well preserved. It removes spurs, loose cartilage and inflamed lining. It does not regrow cartilage and is not a solution for advanced, bone-on-bone arthritis. AAOS OrthoInfo also cautions that removing spurs can increase movement and may speed up cartilage wear in some ankles. Read more about keyhole surgery.

sections.heading: How do ankle fusion and ankle replacement differ?
sections.body:
Ankle fusion (arthrodesis) joins the shin bone and ankle bone into one solid bone, removing the painful movement. Total ankle replacement replaces the worn surfaces with metal and plastic parts so the ankle keeps some movement. Both aim to relieve pain; they differ in movement, long-term wear and the type of complications.

AAOS OrthoInfo notes that after fusion, nearby foot joints take extra stress and may develop arthritis years later. A replacement implant can loosen or wear out, which may need revision surgery or later conversion to a fusion, and that conversion is more difficult.

sections.heading: What did the TARVA trial show?
sections.body:
TARVA is the main randomised trial comparing the two operations. It included 282 people aged 50 to 85 from 17 UK hospitals. At one year, both groups had similar improvements in standing, walking and quality of life, and the overall rate of serious side effects was similar: 18% after replacement and 24% after fusion, according to the NIHR Evidence summary.

The complications differed: wound problems and nerve injuries were more common after replacement, while failure of the bones to join and blood clots were more common after fusion. In a separate analysis, fixed-bearing replacements did better than fusion but mobile-bearing ones did not. The important limitation is that follow-up was only one year; longer-term results are planned at 2, 5 and 10 years.

sections.heading: Which operation is right for me?
sections.body:
There is no single right answer. Either operation is likely to reduce pain and improve quality of life, so the decision rests on your ankle's alignment and bone quality, the health of the joints around it, your age and activity, your skin and circulation, and which set of risks you are more comfortable with.

Points that often come up in discussion:
bullets: Arthritis already present in the neighbouring foot joints may tilt the balance towards replacement, as the TARVA authors suggested
A badly deformed or unstable ankle, poor bone quality or previous infection may make replacement less suitable
Smoking, diabetes and poor skin over the ankle raise the risk of wound and bone-healing problems with either operation
Expectations about heavy work, sport, squatting or floor sitting should be discussed openly with the surgeon before choosing
Not every hospital offers ankle replacement; ask where the operation would be done and by whom

faqs.q: Can ankle arthritis be managed without surgery?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Activity changes, weight loss, supportive or stiff-soled shoes, braces, physiotherapy and anti-inflammatory medicines help many people. A cortisone injection can relieve pain, but the effect is often temporary. Surgery is considered when these measures no longer control pain that limits daily life.

faqs.q: Will I walk normally after an ankle fusion?
faqs.a: Most people walk comfortably after fusion, and the TARVA trial found similar improvement in standing and walking at one year compared with ankle replacement. The ankle itself no longer moves, so uneven ground and slopes may feel different, and nearby foot joints may wear faster over the years.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after ankle fusion or replacement?
faqs.a: AAOS OrthoInfo describes a cast and leg elevation early on, a return to most daily activities in about 3 to 4 months, and full recovery taking 4 to 9 months. Recovery after ankle replacement generally follows a similar timeline.

faqs.q: Does an ankle replacement last forever?
faqs.a: No. The implant can loosen or wear over time, and some patients need revision surgery or conversion to a fusion, which is more difficult than a first-time fusion. Long-term TARVA results are still awaited, so the comparison over 10 years or more is not yet settled.
